public_rationale: The claim has two parts. The shutdown part is documented. Reuters reported on May 21, 2026 that Starbucks retired its 'Automated Counting' AI tool that week, citing an internal newsletter dated Monday, May 18. The tool had been deployed nine months earlier (e1). The same article says Reuters reported in February that the tool frequently miscounted and mislabeled items (e1). Starbucks shared employee feedback that 'the execution was proving difficult' (e2). The causal part is not settled. In its May 21 statement, Starbucks said the decision came from a wish to 'standardize how inventory is counted across coffeehouses' (e3). Reuters reports the errors and the shutdown side by side but does not say the errors caused the shutdown (e1). The company's stated reason does not rule out accuracy concerns, and no cited source confirms them as the cause. So the evidence neither confirms nor contradicts Marcus's statement that Starbucks ended the tool 'because they realized that it couldn't be trusted.'
limitations: No source in the packet gives Starbucks's internal reasoning for the decision.
The company statement is the only direct account of the reason, and it does not mention accuracy.
All three evidence items come from one Reuters article, read through a syndicated copy on a local outlet.
The February Reuters report on miscounts is known only through its summary in the May 21 article.

our_interpretation: Two parts: (1) Starbucks ended its AI inventory tool shortly before May 26, 2026; (2) it did so because the tool's counts were unreliable.
Part (2) is supported if the company or credible reporting ties the shutdown to the tool's errors. It is weakened if the company gives a different reason and no source confirms the stated cause.
criteria.support_condition: Reports that Starbucks ended the AI counting tool around May 2026, and that the decision was driven by its miscounts.
criteria.contradiction_condition: The tool was not ended, or credible evidence shows the decision was made for reasons unrelated to accuracy.

evidence.excerpt: The app – designed to improve ‌Starbucks’ visibility into shortages at stores – frequently miscounted and mislabeled items, such as confusing similar milk types or missing them altogether, Reuters reported in February.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the tool was terminated in the week of May 18, 2026, and that it had a documented record of frequent miscounts. This supports the unreliability part.

evidence.excerpt: “Thanks for discontinuing Automatic Counting! The thought behind it was great, but the execution was proving difficult,” read one.
evidence.explanation: Feedback that Starbucks itself shared points to practical problems with the tool.

evidence.excerpt: Starbucks ⁠said the termination of the program – which covered milk and other beverage products – came from a decision to “standardize how inventory is counted across coffeehouses as we continue to focus on consistency and execution at scale.”
evidence.explanation: Starbucks's official reason was standardizing its process, not that the tool could not be trusted. This cuts against the stated cause.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: An internal document, executive statement, or credible reporting that says whether the tool's accuracy problems were the reason Starbucks retired it, or that shows the decision was made for unrelated reasons.
